title: Field Tech Enablement Quickcompendium (draft)
body:
Purpose:
A compact, practical deck + pocket battle snippets for SEs and field engineers who need to run fast technical conversations (10–15 minute) with integration architects. Focus is on inference economics, predictable SLAs, and fallback strategy — sketched as a one-page rapid-play and a micro-runbook for pilot handoffs.

Status note (draft):
- Intended as a scratchpad for SE rehearsals and quick reference during calls.
- Not final: need input from runtime team on exact latency numbers for r5/4x3 configs and from pricing on committed vs burst tiers.

Slide 0: 30s opener (what we do)
- Headline: "Make inference predictable: latency, cost, and fallbacks you can operate"
- Hook: "If you need consistent p99 latency and clear cost controls across hosted/dedicated/private, here’s how teams do it with Redwood"
- Speaker cue: call out a recent customer: "Fintech KYC flow cut inference cost 32% on day 1 using prefix caching + smaller quantized variant" (internal case — anonymize)

Slide 1: Quick value map (engineer-first)
- Predictable latency: dedicated pools, traffic shaping, regional routing
- Cost levers: batching + KV caching + model variant routing
- Compliance/Isolation: private deployment + per-route logging
- Cue: ask "Which of these is your immediate pain? latency, unpredictability, or cost spikes?"

Slide 2: Runtime sketch (one-line)
- Continuous batching + KV cache + model variant mesh
- Fallback policy: cheapest compatible model -> regional fallback -> cached response -> degrade gracefully
- Cue: emphasize that fallbacks are policy controlled per-route (customer can pin)

Slide 3: Pilot 10-day micro-plan (engineering-friendly)
- Day 0: baseline: sample 1k calls with existing stack (collect seq length dist, token counts, p50/p95/p99)
- Day 1–2: mirror traffic to Redwood hosted sandbox, enable KV caching read-only
- Day 3–5: try Dedicated baseline (small pool) + measure tail latency under synthetic spikes
- Day 6–8: enable batching + quantized variant for non-critical routes; measure cost delta
- Day 9–10: roll canary, set rollback thresholds, handoff to SRE
- Deliverable: 1 page SLO report + cost delta table

Slide 4: One-page fallback quickmap (speaking notes below)
- Primary route: customer model pinned (low latency)
- Fallback 1: compatible quantized variant in same region (saves cost)
- Fallback 2: model variant with shorter context length (reduces kernel runtime)
- Fallback 3: cross-region if capacity constrained (trade latency)
- Fallback 4: pre-canned cached answer for deterministic prompts
- Note: show economic impact in tokens/second for each fallback (placeholder numbers)

Speaker notes for fallback quickmap:
- When to use each: if p99 rises > SLA threshold for 2 consecutive minutes, shift to Fallback 1; if still high, Fallback 2 and notify via webhook + slack channel.
- Testing tactic: inject controlled latencies during canary to validate automatic switch and rollback.

Slide 5: Rapid objection scripts (30–60s answers)
- "We can self-host cheaper": "Cheaper at scale is possible, but our value is operational risk reduction, predictable tail latency, and built-in routing/fallbacks you’d otherwise need months to implement. We help you ship while you iterate on longer-term self-hosting plans."
- "Quantization hurts quality": "We recommend a graded rollout: eval set + user-facing guardrails. For many tasks you get negligible quality loss with 4-bit quantized variants; we run automatic regression checks against your prompts."
- "Vendor lock-in concern": "Route policies are config-first and portable — you can pin model versions, export configs, and run the same runtime privately. We provide exportable artifacts for handoff."

Slide 6: Mini case vignette (micro-case)
- Vertical: customer support automation for a SaaS firm
- Problem: inconsistent p99 during peak onboarding periods
- Approach: mirror traffic -> enable prefix caching -> route non-critical summarization to quantized model -> result: p99 dropped 41%, cost per ticket fell by 27%
- Ask: can we run a similar 1-week mirror + canary?

Slide 7: Pilot success criteria (simple)
- Latency: p99 improvement or stay within SLA with expected traffic
- Cost: demonstrable per-token cost delta or reduced peak spend
- Quality: no >2% regression on labeled eval set
- Ops: automated rollback and alerting in place

Slide 8: Short checklist for pre-call prep (SE)
- Bring: sample logs (JSON requests), representative prompt set (10–20), current SLOs, contact for infra/SRE
- Verify: answer size distribution, common sequence lengths, and tokenization anomalies
- Quick command snippets: (placeholder) collect sequence distribution: "scripts/collect-seq-dist --from=prod --limit=1000"

Appendix: quick triage matrix
- If cost spikes but latency ok: look at batch sizing + caching TTLs
- If latency spikes and cost spikes: try regional autoscale or smaller model variant for low-priority routes
- If tail-only problems: KV cache warm strategies + warmup traffic during deploys

Open TODOs / Decision points
- Get concrete latency profiles on r5/4x3 equivalent for our most common models (ask serving-runtime)
- Confirm pricing delta for Dedicated commit tiers vs burst for the pilot account
- Create an eval set and labeler owner for quality regression checks

Quick links / references
- Confluence: /display/GT/Inference+Pilot+Runbook (placeholder)
- Jira: GT-987 pilot epic (linked above)
- PR: pilot-scripts PR 62 (github link above)

Notes to self:
- Keep this under one slide deck in final: condense quickmap + pilot plan to single page for execs; keep the rest in the SE pocketbook.
- Practice 3x the 3 objection scripts until they feel natural.

End of draft.
